question: What lets you recognise a theme after Chopin has added more voices around it?
intro: The Fourth Ballade does not merely alternate its ideas: it varies them, adds answering voices and changes their harmonic surroundings. Frank Lévy’s broad performance leaves room to hear how a simple song becomes increasingly intricate before the quiet chords and rapid coda.

sections.label: A′ · First theme in counterpoint
sections.mNote: the first theme returns with imitative answering voices

sections.label: B′ · Second theme expanded
sections.mNote: the second theme returns in D♭ with fuller accompaniment

cues.title: An introduction without the tonic
cues.text: The opening invitation centres on C major rather than immediately settling in F minor. It prepares the first song without giving away the full tonal character of the work; remember its melodic contour for its later return.
cues.evidence: C-major introductory harmony in the public Joseffy score, bars 1–7: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/ChopinFF/O52/ballade-4/ballade-4-lys/ballade-4.ly . The opening report windows support timing, not the harmonic identification.

cues.title: A song to remember
cues.text: The first theme introduces the F-minor centre with a restrained, songlike line. Its outline matters more than any single decoration: later variations keep that identity while adding movement and other voices.
cues.evidence: First-theme region begins just after the 0:30 boundary, following a very quiet 0:30 window; variation principle: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep the melody separate
cues.text: Listen for the long melodic line within the shorter notes around it. The accompaniment can become busier without the theme itself becoming quicker; this distinction will help when the writing grows more intricate.
cues.evidence: Listening method for the first-theme variation region, not an exact local scoring claim.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A work of 1842
cues.text: Chopin composed the Fourth Ballade in 1842. Its combination of song, variation and interweaving voices belongs to a period when he was finding increasingly elaborate forms within music for one pianist.
cues.evidence: Date and the work’s variation/polyphonic construction: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

cues.title: Changing the surroundings
cues.text: The first-theme region repeatedly changes the melody’s accompaniment. Follow what stays recognisable through those changes: a variation need not announce a new tune to create a new stage in the argument.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski’s account of variation as a governing principle: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor. Passage cue within the extended first-theme region, not a specific variation boundary.

cues.title: Listen between the extremes
cues.text: As the texture fills out, try listening between the highest notes and the bass. An answering line can become important without becoming the loudest voice in the keyboard texture.
cues.evidence: Listening invitation for the documented polyphonic texture; does not assert a particular entry at 2:55.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A theme can accumulate
cues.text: Chopin can renew a melody by placing more motion around it instead of replacing it. Compare the present density with the first quiet F-minor statement, keeping the main phrase distinct from its elaboration.
cues.evidence: First-theme transformations and increasingly elaborate accompaniment described in https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor. Placement is broad rather than bar-aligned.

cues.title: A Parisian dedication
cues.text: The Ballade is dedicated to Baroness Charlotte de Rothschild. The dedication places this intricate concert work within Chopin’s Parisian network; it is not evidence that the music illustrates her life or a particular occasion.
cues.evidence: Dedicatee listed in the NIFC work record: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

cues.title: Make room for another song
cues.text: After the elaboration of the first theme, listen for a broader, more chordal kind of melody. The second theme’s gently swaying rhythm gives a different shape to the same compound metre.
cues.evidence: Estimated approach to the second theme near 4:45; report shows a lull at 4:30–4:40 followed by B-flat-major-coloured windows. NIFC identifies the second theme as a B-flat-major sicilienne: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The second theme expands
cues.text: The new song does not remain an isolated episode. Its continuation grows into more active writing, allowing the two thematic worlds to become part of one developing span.
cues.evidence: Second-theme continuation and development in Tomaszewski’s description: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor. No specific internal join is claimed at 5:15.

cues.title: More attacks, not another metre
cues.text: The central span is much more densely articulated than the first quiet statement. Listen for a phrase continuing through that activity rather than treating every run as a new musical sentence.
cues.evidence: Report has strong novelty around 5:42 and high onset density around 5:30–6:00. Density is used as a listening anchor, not evidence of a metre or tempo change.

cues.title: No authorised story
cues.text: This Ballade has attracted literary interpretations, but an exact plot from Mickiewicz is not established. The score offers a more secure sequence to follow: introduction, varied themes, returns, a pause and a coda.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski discusses proposed literary interpretation without establishing a programme: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

cues.title: The introduction is remembered
cues.text: The introductory idea returns in a different tonal setting, A major. A familiar contour can serve as a point of recognition even when its new harmony does not bring the music back to the opening’s place.
cues.evidence: Strong report boundary at 6:48 supports approximate placement. A-major introductory return and cadenza in the public Joseffy score, bars 129–134: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/ChopinFF/O52/ballade-4/ballade-4-lys/ballade-4.ly . These bars identify the passage but are not aligned to this recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The theme answers itself
cues.text: The first theme returns with imitative voices: one line can answer another rather than merely sit above chordal support. Try to follow a single strand before combining the voices into the whole texture.
cues.evidence: Approximate return after the 7:20 low-level cadenza region. NIFC describes the canonic return following the introduction: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variation and counterpoint
cues.text: Variation changes a theme’s setting; counterpoint combines distinguishable melodic lines. Tomaszewski identifies both as essential to this Ballade. They explain why a return can be recognisable yet contain more information than its first statement.
cues.evidence: Analytical context, not an event at this instant: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

cues.title: A familiar line inside activity
cues.text: The later first-theme region layers more motion around material heard earlier. Listen for the melody’s direction and phrase lengths rather than trying to give equal attention to every accompanying note.
cues.evidence: Listening invitation in the later variation region; no invented exact voice entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The other song returns
cues.text: The second theme returns in a fuller setting, now in D♭ major. Compare the breadth of its melody with the first appearance: the surrounding activity has changed more drastically than the tune’s basic identity.
cues.evidence: Approximate report boundary at 9:24. D♭-major second-theme return in the public Joseffy score, bars 169 onward: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/ChopinFF/O52/ballade-4/ballade-4-lys/ballade-4.ly . The score establishes the harmony; report windows only support approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A broad late crescendo
cues.text: The returning second-theme span gathers sustained weight. Listen for the longer dynamic direction across many phrases, not only the smaller rises and falls within each one.
cues.evidence: Report levels rise from −12.6 dB at 9:25 to −8.4 at 10:15 and −5.3 at 10:25; a broad contour, not a claim about a written crescendo’s exact start.

cues.title: The crest is not the ending
cues.text: The large late crest still leaves an entire coda ahead. Listen for how the momentum is interrupted before that final stretch, rather than assuming the loudest expansion supplies an immediate conclusion.
cues.evidence: Strong late windows at 10:20–10:40 are followed by a sharp drop around 10:45. Formal succession to quiet chords and coda: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

cues.title: Quiet chords hold the space
cues.text: After the accumulated motion, quiet separated chords suspend the momentum. They are not the final resolution: their restraint makes the much faster coda sound newly exposed when it starts.
cues.evidence: Report shows very low level and few attacks from 10:45 to 11:10, before the 11:14 boundary. Quiet chords before the coda are documented in https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep a larger pulse
cues.text: In the rapid coda, listen through the many small attacks for the larger accented groups. The busy surface can otherwise hide the direction towards the final F-minor close.
cues.evidence: Listening invitation within the coda, placed after the clearly denser 11:14 boundary; no specific accent is timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: No return to the invitation
cues.text: The coda finishes in the work’s F-minor centre. Unlike the earlier return of the introduction, this conclusion does not reopen the lyrical discussion: its concentrated figuration carries the piece to final chords.
cues.evidence: Concluding function and F-minor ending of the score; NIFC work commentary https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor. The report places final sounding material before the decay after 12:30.

transitions.title: The invitation gives way to a quiet song
transitions.how: The C-centred introduction withdraws and the first theme establishes the Ballade’s F-minor world. A more regular songlike phrase takes the foreground. This is a change of function as well as key: the introduction has invited attention, while the new melody supplies material for the later variations.
transitions.evidence: Boundary 0:30 and very quiet 0:30 window anchor the approximate change; thematic design: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

transitions.title: Elaboration opens onto a broader melody
transitions.how: After the first theme has acquired increasingly elaborate surroundings, a second song appears in B♭ major. Its chordal, gently swaying character offers a different kind of continuity from the first theme’s variations. The compound metre remains a common ground despite the change in melodic profile.
transitions.evidence: Approximate boundary follows quieter 4:30–4:40 windows and a B-flat-major region from 4:45; NIFC describes the sicilienne: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

transitions.title: Development recalls the opening invitation
transitions.how: The developing middle span recovers the introduction’s contour in A major. This is not a simple return to the original tonal starting point: recognition comes from the melody, while the transposition withholds a return to F minor. A cadenza-like continuation then clears space for the first theme.
transitions.evidence: Strong report boundary at 6:48 anchors approximate timing. A-major return and cadenza in the public Joseffy score, bars 129–134: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/ChopinFF/O52/ballade-4/ballade-4-lys/ballade-4.ly . NIFC documents the returning introduction’s formal function.

transitions.title: The song returns with answering voices
transitions.how: After the introductory return and its cadenza, the first theme reappears in an imitative texture. What was originally heard as a song with support now participates in a conversation between melodic lines. The return is therefore a new stage of development rather than a reset.
transitions.evidence: The 7:20 low-level window and ensuing activity anchor the approximate return. Imitative construction and the initially transposed theme before F minor is recovered are visible in the public Joseffy score, bars 135–140 onward: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/ChopinFF/O52/ballade-4/ballade-4-lys/ballade-4.ly . No immediate F-minor return is inferred from chroma.

transitions.title: The second song takes a larger space
transitions.how: The first theme’s renewed elaboration leads to the second theme in D♭ major. The melody broadens over fuller accompaniment, giving its return more weight than the first B♭-major appearance. Familiar thematic shape and changed harmony are heard together rather than as separate events.
transitions.evidence: Approximate report boundary at 9:24; the score, not chroma, establishes the D♭-major second-theme return. Public Joseffy score, bars 169 onward: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/ChopinFF/O52/ballade-4/ballade-4-lys/ballade-4.ly .

transitions.title: The accumulated force is withheld
transitions.how: The broad late climax stops short of the final coda. Quiet, separated chords replace the preceding density, stretching the sense of waiting. Their sparse texture is a structural interruption: the ear has time to register the change before rapid motion begins again.
transitions.evidence: Report drops from loud 10:35–10:40 windows to −37.3 dB with almost no attacks at 10:45, remaining quiet through 11:10.

transitions.title: Sparse chords release rapid motion
transitions.how: The quiet chordal link gives way to the coda’s continuous rapid figuration. The contrast is not a gradual thickening of the same accompaniment: pulse, register and density are reorganised at once. The ensuing span drives towards the F-minor close rather than another lyrical return.
transitions.evidence: Report boundary 11:14; level rises from −34.2 dB at 11:10 to −10.6 at 11:15 and onset density increases sharply; coda function: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
